questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: A system scores better than doctors at spotting one type of spot on X-rays. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: It will also be excellent at reading patient notes
It can now replace doctors for all medical decisions

questions.correct_answer: It did well on that narrow task; other tasks need checks
questions.intro: People often compare AI with humans: "it reads," "it thinks," "it is like a student." Comparisons can help explain a new idea, but they can also mislead. A system may beat experts at one narrow task, such as spotting a pattern in thousands of images, yet fail at something a child finds easy, like counting objects in an unusual picture. Its abilities can be UNEVEN in ways a human's are not, so success on one task does not predict success on a nearby task. Treat a human comparison as a starting point, then check how the system actually performs on the task you care about.
questions.feedback: Narrow success does not transfer automatically.

sections.skill: Compare uneven skill to a calculator and a toddler

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: What can the calculator do better than a person?

choices.text: Tell a cat from a dog at a glance
Explain a joke
Multiply huge numbers quickly
Learn a language

questions.correct_answer: Multiply huge numbers quickly
questions.intro: A pocket calculator multiplies huge numbers instantly, faster than any person, yet it cannot tell a cat from a dog. A toddler easily tells a cat from a dog but cannot multiply 27 by 43. Neither is "smarter" overall; they have different abilities. AI systems are similar: a system can be impressive at one thing and weak at another, in a pattern unlike any human's. So ask "How good is it at THIS task?" rather than "How smart is it?"

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Describe what was observed instead of "smart" or "dumb"

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: A chatbot answers warmly, "I totally understand how you feel." What should you keep in mind?

choices.text: Friendly wording does not show feelings or judgment
It is lying, so nothing it says is useful
Friendly replies are always more accurate than others
It must truly share your feelings

questions.correct_answer: Friendly wording does not show feelings or judgment
questions.intro: Human comparisons shape trust. If a system "sounds like a person," people may assume it has human judgment, feelings or common sense. Some language models are trained to sound helpful and friendly, which can make errors easier to miss. On the other hand, dismissing a system as "just a machine" can hide real abilities and real risks. A better habit is to describe what was observed: "It summarized these ten reports accurately but invented one date," rather than "It is smart" or "It is dumb." Specific observations can be checked.
questions.feedback: Sounding human can raise trust without evidence.
